records.quote: Corollary 3.6 Assume the functional T and the generator of the Archimedean copula describing the distribution of X are such that the function V defined in (4) (with ψ2 = ψ1) is increasing. Fix numbers a < b and c ∈ [na, nb), and define Aa,b,c = {α = (α1,...,αn) ∈ [a,b]^n : Σ_{i=1}^n αi = c}, ᾱ = (c/n,...,c/n), q = ⌊(c − na)/(b − a)⌋, and η = c − qb − (n − q − 1)a. Then η ∈ [a, b) and α∗ = (a,...,a [n−q−1 times], η, b,...,b [q times]) ∈ Aa,b,c. Moreover, for every α ∈ Aa,b,c, Xn:n(α∗) ≥st Xn:n(α) ≥st Xn:n(ᾱ).

records.quote: Example 3.17 Take E(x) = 1 − e^{−x}, for x ≥ 0, the standard exponential, and the functional T(α, E)(x) = 1−(1−E(x))^α = 1−e^{−αx}, where α > 0. Consider a system with n = 3 components with lifetimes T(αi, E), for i = 1, 2, 3, whose joint distribution is described by an Archimedean copula with Clayton generator ψ(t) = (1 + t)^{−1}, for t ≥ 0. With α = (α1, α2, α3), the lifetime of a 2-out-of-3 system is X2:3(α), whose distribution function is obtained by using (12): F^{(α)}_{2:3}(x) = ψ(t1 + t2) + ψ(t1 + t3) + ψ(t2 + t3) − 2ψ(t1 + t2 + t3), where ti = (e^{αi x} − 1)^{−1}. A direct differentiation with respect to αℓ gives ∂F^{(α)}_{2:3}(x)/∂αℓ = t'ℓ (Σ_{j≠ℓ} ψ'(tℓ + tj) − 2ψ'(t1 + t2 + t3)), where t'ℓ = −xe^{αℓ x}(e^{αℓ x} −1)^{−2}. Choosing now α = (1, 2.5, 4), the plots for (αℓ − αm)(∂F_{2:3}/∂αℓ − ∂F_{2:3}/∂αm) are shown in Figure 1. Although when taking (ℓ, m) = (1, 3) or (2, 3) the curve has a constant sign, the case (ℓ, m) = (1, 2) changes sign as x ranges (0, +∞). Hence, the map α ↦ F^{(α)}_{2:3}(x) is neither Schur-convex nor Schur-concave.

records.quote: Example 3.5 As an application of the previous results, choose as baseline the standard exponential distribution E(x) = 1−e^{−x}, for x ≥ 0, and, for β > 0, T(β, E)(x) = 1−(1−E(x))^β = 1−e^{−βx}, the exponential distribution with hazard rate β. Then, with the notation of Theorems 3.1 and 3.3, X = (X1,...,Xn) and Y = (Y1,...,Yn) are random vectors with dependent components whose marginal distributions are heterogeneous exponentials. Assume the distributions of X and Y are described using a Clayton copula with parameters γ1 and γ2, respectively, such that γ2 ≥ γ1 > 0. Then, as referred in Example 2.6, ϕ2 ◦ ψ1 is super-additive. Hence, from Theorem 3.1, if αi ≤ βi, i = 1,...,n, it follows that Xn:n(α) ≥st Yn:n(β). In case we do not have increasing coordinates for the parameter vectors, but they still satisfy α ⪰^m β, we get a conclusion using Theorem 3.3. Moreover, for the Clayton generator ψ2' ◦ ϕ2(T(β, E))(x) = −(1 − e^{−x})^{1+γ2}, so V(β) = −x(1 − e^{−βx})^{−(1+γ2)} e^{−βx}, which is increasing with respect to β > 0, so again we conclude that Xn:n(α) ≥st Yn:n(β).

records.quote: Lemma 2.4 (Li and Fang (2015), Lemma A.1) For two n-dimensional Archimedean copulas Cψ1 and Cψ2, if ϕ2 ◦ ψ1 is super-additive, then Cψ1(u) ≤ Cψ2(u), for u ∈ [0, 1]^n.

records.quote: Example 2.5 Assume that ψ1(t) = e^{−t}, the generator of the independence copula. For generators ψ2 within the above-mentioned families, the super-additivity assumption holds for a wide range of parameter values. 1. The Clayton case with γ2 ≥ 0: ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = (e^{γ2 t} − 1)/γ2, convex, and ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(0) = 0, so super-additivity follows. 2. The Frank case with γ2 > 0: ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = −log[(e^{−t}(e^{−γ2} − 1) + 1)/(e^{−γ2} − 1)], convex for t ≥ 0. 3. The Gumbel case with γ2 ≥ 1: ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = t^{γ2}, super-additive on [0, ∞). 4. The AMH case with γ2 ∈ (0, 1): ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = log[(1 − γ2(1 − e^{−t}))/e^{−t}] = log((1 − γ2)e^t + γ2), convex with ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(0) = 0.

records.quote: Example 2.6 Consider now two generators ψ1 and ψ2 from the same family of copulas, with parameters γ1 and γ2. With the appropriate range of variability for the parameters, the composition ϕ2 ◦ ψ1 is still super-additive. 1. The Clayton family with γ2 ≥ γ1 > 0: ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = (1/γ1)((1 + γ1 t)^{γ2/γ1} − 1), convex, hence super-additive. 2. The Frank copulas with γ2 ≥ γ1: ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = −log[((e^{−t}(e^{−γ1} − 1) + 1)^{γ2/γ1} − 1)/(e^{−γ2} − 1)], convex. 3. The Gumbel family with γ2 ≥ γ1 ≥ 1: ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = t^{γ2/γ1}, convex and null at the origin, super-additive. 4. The AMH copulas with 1 ≥ γ2 ≥ γ1 ≥ 0: ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = log[(1−γ2)/(1−γ1) e^t + (γ2−γ1)/(1−γ1)] =: log(a e^t + b).

records.quote: Example 4.12 We showed in Example 2.6 that the super-additivity assumption is fulfilled composing two different copulas within the same family. We now show that the Gumbel family allows for some more flexibility on the choice of the copula ψ1. Choose ψ1(t) = exp(−t − ct^2), for some c > 0. Clearly, ψ1 is decreasing, ψ1(0) = 1 and ψ1(t) → 0 as t → ∞. Moreover, it is completely monotone and therefore defines a valid Archimedean copula. Then, ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = (− log ψ1(t))^{γ2} = (t + ct^2)^{γ2}. Taking γ2 > 1, this is an increasing and convex transformation of a super-additive function, hence it is super-additive.

records.quote: Example 4.13 Concerning the super-additivity assumption in Proposition 4.11 when using a AMH generator, we have already verified that we may choose for ψ1 the independent copula or another copula within the AMH family. We show next that we may also take ψ1 within the Gumbel class. Let ψ1(t) = exp(−t^{1/α}), α ≥ 1, be the generator function of the Gumbel family of copulas, and assume γ2 > 0. Then ϕ2 ◦ ψ1(t) = log[(1 − γ2(1 − e^{−t^{1/α}}))/e^{−t^{1/α}}] = log[(1 − γ2)e^{t^{1/α}} + γ2] =: gα(t). ... which proves that gα is super-additive.
